inline.s: From this time on (beginning with the Sixth Patriarch), Chan’s sons and grandsons filled the eye and spread throughout the world; those who obtained it had their thought and emotion die, those who lost it had ignorance arise; the seventeen hundred (referring to the seventeen hundred public cases), piping and playing, did no more than mutually illuminate one another in this mind-ground Dharma gate — where was it that outside this mind one should seek a wondrous awakening? If one seeks elsewhere apart from this, one falls into the crooked paths of outside teachings. Hence the Brahmā Net Sutra says: “The mind-ground of Vairocana Buddha, recited in the first arising of the mind, is named the Precept of Radiant Vajra Precious Precepts; it is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all bodhisattvas, the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings have Buddha-nature; all consciousness, form, and mind, whatever is feeling and whatever is mind, all enter the precept of Buddha-nature.” It also says: “When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they at once enter the rank of all Buddhas; their rank being equal to great awakening, they are truly the sons of the Buddhas.” Therefore in the fifty-five stages of progressive practice, one who has not seen Buddha-nature falls upon the road of stages. Only when at the very end, in the stage of equal awakening, does it say: “This person first obtains the vajra mind, the initial stage of dry wisdom, and arriving here enters directly into the ocean of Buddha-nature.” [The fifty-five stages of progressive practice] That is, the fifty-five Mahāyāna stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dwelling, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the four preparatory practices, the ten grounds, and equal awakening. [The four preparatory practices] In the course of Mahāyāna practice, between the ten dedications and the ten grounds one must still pass through the four preparatory practices as preparation for entering the first ground. The so-called four preparatory practices are the cultivation of the four investigations, by which the four kinds of true wisdom are obtained. “Preparatory practice” means that when one is about to enter the proper stage of cultivation, one must add a stretch of effort to one’s practice. [Piping and playing (gǔ huáng)] To blow the sheng. The huáng is the copper reed in the pipes of a sheng, and by extension the sheng itself; it is used as a metaphor for clever words and fine argument. [The stage of dry wisdom] The first of the “ten common grounds of the three vehicles” among the bodhisattva stages of practice; on this ground there is wisdom but no concentration, and so it is called the stage of dry wisdom.

[Seen in this way, apart from this vajra mind, is there any other essential dharma for going from ordinary to sage, for becoming a Buddha and a patriarch? Know then that these precepts are not easy to awaken to: to awaken is to be named the stage of dwelling. They are not easy to practice: to practice is to be named the stage of practice. They are not easy to penetrate: to penetrate is to be named the stage of dedication. They are not easy to purify: to purify is to be named the stage of the grounds. They are not easy to forget: to forget is to be named the stage of entering Buddhahood.]

Seen in this way, apart from this vajra mind, what other path is there for going from ordinary to sage and becoming a Buddha and a patriarch? Know then that these precepts are not easy to awaken to: to awaken is to be named the stage of the ten dwellings. They are not easy to practice: to practice is to be named the stage of the ten practices. They are not easy to penetrate: to penetrate is to be named the stage of the ten dedications. They are not easy to purify: to purify is to be named the stage of the ten grounds. They are not easy to forget: to forget is to be named the stage of entering Buddhahood.

[The fifty-two stages] From ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages in all: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dwelling, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal awakening, and wondrous awakening (Buddhahood).

[Fasheng, today you should truly examine yourself: with what mind did you leave home? With what mind do you call on teachers and visit friends? With what mind do you delight in seeking the Buddhadharma? With what mind are you willing to receive these precepts? If you get at that mind, then the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all sentient beings together will emit light and shake the earth from the tip of a single hair of the Elder, and then in the twelve periods of the day you will be joined eyebrow to eyebrow with all sages and ordinary beings. This is what is called truly upholding the precepts. Otherwise there is danger, and where there is danger one falls. Investigate! Investigate! Investigate! (Original note: Dongwen first took Iron-Beak Lanfeng as his teacher. The “Water-Flood Crane” mentioned here refers to Lanfeng.)]

Fasheng, today you should earnestly search your own heart: with what mind did you leave home? With what mind do you call on teachers and visit friends? With what mind do you delight in seeking the Buddhadharma? With what mind are you willing to receive these precepts? If you get at that mind, then the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all sentient beings together will emit light and shake the earth from the tip of a single hair of the Elder, and then in the twelve periods of the day you will be joined eyebrow to eyebrow with all sages and ordinary beings. This is what is called truly upholding the precepts. Otherwise there is danger, and where there is danger one falls. Investigate! Investigate! Investigate!

[The tip of a single hair] The Avataṃsaka Sutra says: “Entering right concentration within a single pore, from that concentration emerging through all pores; entering right concentration through all pores, from that concentration emerging at the tip of a single hair.” This is the state of “manifesting a Buddha-land at the tip of a single hair, turning the great Dharma wheel within a single mote of dust.” Master Hanshan’s The Dream-Wandering Collection

Record of the Restoration of the Stupa Court of Master Wan at Shijing Mountain in Zhuozhou says: “Thus our Buddha, the World-Honored One, throughout vast kalpas gazed upon the worlds of the ten directions, and there was not so much as a mustard seed’s worth where he did not give up body and life for sentient beings’ sake, seeking the place of this Dharma; and having just sought and obtained it, he manifests a Buddha-land at the tip of a single hair and turns the great Dharma wheel within a single mote of dust.”

blocks.text: 41. No Quarrel Between Chan and Pure Land

inline.s: The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan monk Huijing Xin

[Our Buddha taught the Dharma with the one mind as the core. No matter how many hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates there are, none is other than a practice for realizing the one mind. The most essential of them are simply Chan practice and Buddha-recitation. Chan practice is the method for awakening to the mind established by the patriarchs of former times in this land; the gate of Buddha-recitation is what our Buddha revealed to the bodhisattvas of the three worthy ranks and the ten grounds, for whom Buddha-recitation is in every case the essential means of becoming a Buddha. The bodhisattvas of the ten grounds have already realized true suchness — are they not awakened? Yet they all say: never apart from recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, and recollection of the Saṃgha.]

Our Buddha taught the Dharma with the one mind as the core. No matter how many hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates there are, none is other than a practice for realizing the one mind. The most essential of them are simply Chan practice and Buddha-recitation. Chan practice is the method for awakening to the mind established by the patriarchs of former times in this land; the gate of Buddha-recitation is what our Buddha revealed to the bodhisattvas of the three worthy ranks and the ten grounds — in short, taking Buddha-recitation as the essential means of becoming a Buddha. The bodhisattvas of the ten grounds have already realized true suchness — are they not awakened? Yet they all say: never apart from recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, and recollection of the Saṃgha.

[The three worthy ranks] In the course of Mahāyāna practice, among the fifty-two stages from ordinary being to sage, the bodhisattvas of the ten dwellings, ten practices, and ten dedications have cut off only the delusions of views and thoughts and still have the delusions of dust-and-sand and of ignorance; they have not entered the sage stage of the ten grounds, and so are called only the “three worthy ranks,” or “bodhisattvas before the grounds.” [The three delusions] The delusion of views and thoughts, the delusion of dust-and-sand, and the delusion of ignorance. The delusion of views and thoughts is the delusion of ordinary beings: the delusion of views within it is error in understanding and views, such as the five wrong views of view of body, extreme views, and so on; the delusion of thoughts is error in thought, such as the five afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. If those on the paths of the voice-hearers and the solitary realizers cut off these two delusions, they realize the fruit of arhatship and escape the three realms. The delusion of dust-and-sand is the delusion of bodhisattvas: if a bodhisattva who transforms and saves sentient beings does not master the immeasurable Dharma gates, as numerous as dust and sand, he cannot complete the work of teaching sentient beings; hence it is called the delusion of dust-and-sand. The delusion of ignorance is fundamental ignorance, which obscures the principle of the middle way and true reality; when it is cut off entirely, one becomes a Buddha. Among the three delusions, the delusion of views and thoughts is coarse, the dust-and-sand is middling, and ignorance is subtle.

[Sudhana visited fifty-three good friends; the first, the monk Deyun, granted him solely the Dharma gate of liberation through Buddha-recitation. And at the very end, when he visited Samantabhadra, the good friend for entering wondrous awakening, he dedicated it exclusively toward the Pure Land of the West, saying: “Beholding the Tathāgata’s immeasurable light, may he bestow on me the bodhi prediction face to face.” Seen in this way, even though the Avataṃsaka is the highest single vehicle, and its practice is called the practice of the Dharma realm, it is from first to last never apart from Buddha-recitation. Sages of the ten grounds, having already realized true suchness, are still not apart from Buddha-recitation — and yet deluded people of the Dharma-ending age dare to slander Buddha-recitation as an inferior practice! How then can one doubt that Chan practice and Buddha-recitation are in conflict? It is a want
(a variant of the character for “want”)
of broad learning, not knowing the Buddha’s intent, that gives rise to false discrimination.]

Sudhana visited fifty-three good friends; the first, the monk Deyun, granted him solely the Dharma gate of liberation through Buddha-recitation. At the very end he visited Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Samantabhadra, the good friend for entering wondrous awakening, dedicated exclusively toward the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, saying: “Beholding the Tathāgata’s immeasurable light, may he bestow on me the bodhi prediction face to face.” Seen in this way, even if the Avataṃsaka samādhi is the highest single vehicle, and its method of practice is called the gate of practice of the Dharma realm, it is likewise from first to last never apart from Buddha-recitation. Sages of the ten grounds, having already realized true suchness, are still not apart from Buddha-recitation — and yet deluded people of the Dharma-ending age dare to slander Buddha-recitation as an inferior practice! How then can one doubt that Chan practice and Buddha-recitation are in conflict? It is only that they are poorly informed, not knowing the Buddha’s intent, and so give rise to false discrimination.

[Avataṃsaka samādhi] An abbreviation of the Buddha-Avataṃsaka samādhi. Also called Avataṃsaka concentration, it is the Chan concentration entered by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. This samādhi is the great samādhi that encompasses the Dharma realm and contains all Buddhadharmas. [The practice of the Dharma realm] In explaining the essence of Avataṃsaka samādhi, the Record of Profound Investigation of the Avataṃsaka says: “The gate of practice of the Dharma realm takes the ocean of mind as its substance. Through meditative equipoise it is vast and limitless.”

[If one speaks in terms of the Pure Land of mind only, then when the mind is pure the land is pure. Therefore, when one first practices Chan and has not yet awakened, without Buddha-recitation there is no way to purify one’s own mind; yet when the mind is pure, that is awakening to the mind. Bodhisattvas, having awakened, do not abandon Buddha-recitation; so without Buddha-recitation there is no way to perfect enlightenment. How then do we know that the patriarchs did not awaken to the mind through Buddha-recitation? If one recites the Buddha’s name to the point of single-mindedness, with afflictions dissolved and one’s own mind clearly understood, that is named awakening; in that case Buddha-recitation is precisely Chan practice. And as with the bodhisattvas, it means not abandoning Buddha-recitation after awakening. Hence the patriarchs of former times all did not abandon the Pure Land. In this way, Buddha-recitation is precisely Chan practice, and Chan practice is precisely birth in the Pure Land. This has been an unresolved doubt through the ages; now that this explanation has broken it open completely, the view that separates Chan from Pure Land is entirely dissolved. Even if the Buddhas were to appear in the world, they would not speak differently from this. If one sets this aside and gives rise to other wild opinions, all such talk is the talk of demons, not the Buddhadharma.]

If one speaks in terms of the Pure Land of mind only, then when the mind is pure the land is pure. Therefore, when one first practices Chan and has not yet awakened, without Buddha-recitation there is no way to purify one’s own mind; yet when the mind is pure, that is awakening to the mind. Bodhisattvas, having awakened, do not abandon Buddha-recitation; thus without Buddha-recitation there is no way to become a Buddha. How then do we know that the patriarchs did not awaken to the mind through Buddha-recitation? If one recites the Buddha’s name to the point of single-mindedness, with afflictions dissolved and one’s own mind clearly understood, that is named awakening; in that case Buddha-recitation is precisely Chan practice. And as with the bodhisattvas, it means not abandoning Buddha-recitation even after awakening. Hence the patriarchs of former times all did not abandon the Pure Land. In this way, Buddha-recitation is precisely Chan practice, and Chan practice is precisely birth in the Pure Land. The quarrel between Chan and Pure Land has been an unresolved case through the ages. By what has been said above this doubt is thoroughly broken, and the view that separates Chan from Pure Land is from then on entirely dissolved. Even if the Buddhas were to appear in the world, they would have no different teaching. If one sets this aside and gives rise to other wild opinions, all such talk is the talk of demons, not the Buddhadharma.
The Dream-Wandering Collection
Reply to the Military Commander Yang Yuanru

[The ancients said, “In the field of feverish confusion, a cool eye is hard to withstand.” Because the three realms are without safety, like a burning house, none who come and go within them are not scorched and boiled. If one would find a patch of coolness amid the blazing flames, none but a cool-eyed person can obtain it. If one can in a single thought be cool, at once seeing the whole earth as ice, one will naturally no longer take the world of body and mind as a refuge. This is how the people of great strength from of old, playing in the field of birth and death, can turn worldly toil into Buddha-work and transform affliction into bodhi: they rely solely on that one cool eye and that one cool-hearted disposition of theirs — what need is there of any further spiritual powers and wondrous functions?]

The ancients said, “In the field of feverish confusion, though everything churns the mind, it cannot withstand being looked at with a cool eye.” Because the three realms are without safety, like a burning house, none who come and go within them are not scorched and boiled. If one would find a patch of coolness amid the blazing flames, only a cool-eyed person can manage it. If one can look upon the world with a cool eye until a single thought is cool, then at once one sees the whole earth as ice, and naturally will not take the world of body and mind as a refuge. From of old, the people of great strength who play in the field of birth and death and can turn worldly toil into Buddha-work and transform affliction into bodhi rely precisely on that one cool eye and that one cool-hearted disposition of theirs — what further spiritual powers and wondrous functions could there be?

[The three realms are without safety, like a burning house] The Lotus Sutra says: “The three realms are without safety, like a burning house, filled with many sufferings, most terrifying; there are always the sorrows of birth, aging, sickness, and death; such fires blaze without cease.” [They rely solely on that one cool eye and that one cool-hearted disposition] This means: when the mind is empty the object is empty of itself; the ten thousand dharmas bind nothing, and are originally liberated. The Diamond Sutra says: “All that has marks is deceptive.” “Not grasping at marks, one is thus, unmoving.” Of these two lines, “all that has marks is deceptive” is the cool eye; “not grasping at marks, one is thus, unmoving” is the cool heart. In the phrase above, “that” renders the pronoun qu, meaning “he.”

[These words are very easy to know, but very hard to see. Take the case of the Buddhas and patriarchs, who took the single phrase “all dharmas are like a dream” as the essential road out of the world. Yet the wise and the foolish of the world alike can all say, “Life is a dream.” Their words may be alike, but their meaning is not. In fact they have never truly, with one glance, seen through life as a dream. If one really saw through it, one would naturally, at every pass of honor and disgrace, gain and loss, right and wrong, swing one’s arms and walk away — who would dare cross swords with such a one?]

These words (“in the field of feverish confusion, a cool eye is hard to withstand”) are very easy to know, but their true meaning is very hard to see. Just as the Buddhas and patriarchs took the single phrase “all dharmas are like a dream” as the essential road out of the world — but how many see its true meaning? And the wise and the foolish of the world alike can all say, “Life is a dream.” Though the words are the same phrase, “life is a dream,” the meaning in the mouths of the wise and the foolish is entirely different. The foolish say it with their lips, but in fact have never truly, with one glance, seen through life as a dream. If one really saw through it, one would naturally be able to turn and walk away at every pass of honor and disgrace, gain and loss, right and wrong — and who could hold one back? (The carp slips off the golden hook and goes, wagging its head and tail, never to return.)
[Swinging the arms (diào bì)] To swing one’s arms and walk off — to depart without a backward look.

[In fact there is nothing very mysterious in it. As for the first step, however, there is no lack of a method. When we live in the world, we should first take the affairs of the dream and hold them up before our eyes, observing them closely. We must truly and distinctly look until we cannot help but burst into a great laugh. At that point we will suddenly feel that the ordinary saying “like a dream” has a meaning utterly different from before. Then, taking that place of laughter, turn a single thought to the objects before us and place them within the dream, observing closely. When we see them hazy and heavy and upside down, suddenly we wake with a start. In this way, looking back over our life, every kind of object we have ever passed through, when we truly seek it, is utterly unattainable. That place of utter unattainability is precisely the first gate through which the Buddhas and patriarchs leave birth and death.]

In fact there is nothing very mysterious in it. As for taking the first step, there is no lack of a method. The method is this: when we live in the world, we should first take the affairs of the dream and hold them up before our eyes, observing them closely. We must look truly and distinctly, until we cannot help bursting into a great laugh. At that point we will suddenly feel that the ordinary saying “life is a dream” has an utterly different meaning. Then, taking that place of laughing awakening, turn a single thought toward the objects before us and place them within the framework of “life is a dream,” observing closely. When we see them hazy and heavy and upside down, suddenly we wake with a start. In this way, looking back over our life, every kind of object we have ever passed through — even if we wish to take them as real, they are utterly unattainable (we simply cannot manage it). That place of utter unattainability is precisely the first gate through which the Buddhas and patriarchs leave birth and death.
[Looking until one cannot help but burst into a great laugh] Master Hanshan’s Song of Awakening the World says:

‘In life a thousand, ten thousand schemes one spends; in death one leaves an empty pair of hands. Joy, sorrow, parting, meeting — clamor day by day; long life or early death, success or failure — busy day by day. Do not strive for strength and fight to win: a hundred years are all a stage of play. In a moment the gong and drum fall still — who knows where one’s home village lies
(who knows how it will end)

[Do not strive to be strong and fight for victory] A person’s life is like a white colt glimpsed through a crack, gone in the blink of an eye. The result is that “the ten thousand things cannot be taken along; only karma follows the body”: after death the two hands are empty, yet the retribution of the evil karma created by striving for strength and fighting for victory follows like a shadow into future lives. Therefore, do not strive to be strong and fight for victory; rather, use the energy and time spent on such striving for practice, so as to settle birth and death. [A hundred years are wholly a stage of play] A hundred years of life are entirely a play. [In a moment the gong and drum fall silent] In a moment the play is sung out (the gong and drum fall silent).

blocks.text: 43. A Single Thought Turns the Mind Around

inline.s: The Dream-Wandering Collection
To Liu Cunchi

[We have for many lives and accumulated kalpas been sunk in the mud of the five desires and burned by the karmic fire of the seven emotions — deep and fierce indeed. There are no heroes who are not drowned and boiled by them. To seek a single thought that turns the mind around is utterly unattainable, let alone hoping that they will give rise to a mind of detachment, seek the way out of suffering, and single-mindedly rest their minds on the Pure Land in Buddha-recitation. This is not merely a lotus emerging from mud, but a root sending forth from within fire. What joy could be greater!]

From many lives and accumulated kalpas, we have been sunk in the mud of the five desires and burned by the karmic fire of the seven emotions — deep and fierce indeed. There are no heroes who are not drowned and boiled by them. Even to obtain a single thought that turns the mind around is unattainable, let alone hoping that they will give rise to a mind of detachment, seek the way out of suffering, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and rest their minds on the Pure Land. But that you can single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and rest your mind on the Pure Land means it is not merely a red lotus emerging from the mud of the five desires, but a root planted within the karmic fire of the seven emotions. How greatly this rejoices one!

[The five desires] The craving for form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means melodious sounds; smell means fragrant scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means pleasant tactile pleasures. [The seven emotions] Joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, and desire.

[We who wish to escape birth and death must know the root of birth and death. You wish to seek the root of the Pure Land, but you little know that the root of the Pure Land is precisely the root of birth and death. It lies in this mind’s turning around in a single thought — in the span
(the text writes this character for “span”)

between, sparing no effort. May you earnestly fix your eye in advance on the objects before you in daily life: at the time of the reunion of wife and children, in the intervals of dealings with friends, at the point where right and profit attack each other, before joy and anger have arisen — truly and distinctly, clearly and exactly, see what the root of birth and death is, and then at once pull it out with all your might.]

We who wish to escape birth and death must certainly know the root of birth and death. In your letter you say you wish to know the root of cultivating the Pure Land; you little know that the root of cultivating the Pure Land is precisely the pulling out of the root of birth and death. And pulling out the root of birth and death lies in sparing no effort in the interval of a single thought’s turning of this mind! May you carefully fix your eye in advance on the objects before you in daily life: at the time of the reunion of wife and children, in the intervals of dealings with friends, at the point where right and profit attack each other, before joy and anger have arisen — truly and distinctly, clearly and exactly, see what the root of birth and death is, and immediately pull it out with all your might.
[The root of birth and death] Master Hanshan’s The Dream-Wandering Collection

Instructions for Feng Yanling says: “A student who turns toward the Way must first fear birth and death, and second must know the root of birth and death. The root of birth and death is simply the various hatred and love, taking and rejecting, self-conceit, and karma of greed, hatred, and delusion that appear before one in daily life. Since this is the bitter root of birth and death, if one resolves to cut it off there is no other technique: one need only illuminate it the moment it arises and firmly refuse to let it arise.” [Reunion (tuán
luán
)] To come together. [Clearly and exactly] Distinctly.

[Yet our mind is originally pure; what makes it defiled and turbid is in truth the foul grime of this root and stem. If one can uproot it with force, then the Pure Land comes without being sought. What is called “once one root returns to the source, the six faculties are all liberated” refers precisely to this. If one sees through the single fundamental thought, then every matter in daily life is a field of liberation, all returning to the realm of ultimate bliss. Truly, though the body has not yet entered the lotus, the mind is sent ahead to the heaven of ultimate bliss.]

Yet our mind is originally pure; what makes it defiled and turbid is in truth the foul grime of this root of birth and death. If one can uproot it with force, then the Pure Land comes without being sought. What is called “once one root returns to the source, the six faculties are all liberated” refers precisely to this. If one sees through the single fundamental thought, then every single matter in daily life is a field of liberation, all returning to the realm of ultimate bliss. This is truly: though the body has not yet entered the lotus, the mind is sent ahead to the heaven of ultimate bliss.

[Once one root returns to the source, the six faculties are all liberated] From the Śūraṃgama Sutra. It means that among the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), as long as one of them returns to the source, the whole of the six faculties is liberated. Here it is a metaphor for this: as soon as the root of birth and death is pulled out, the whole is liberated.

blocks.text: 44. Do Not Fall into the Illness of Letting Things Be

inline.s: The Dream-Wandering Collection · To Master Xiu Liuyi, Keeper of the Retreat

[The confusion of the past few days, I imagine, has already settled. This matter cannot be done with admixtures; one must lay hold right where the root of life is cut off and simply go on doing it. Do not concern yourself with how he is or how I am: the moment a hairsbreadth remains in the breast, you are toyed with by it. This present karmic opportunity is one that could not be sought in a hundred thousand kalpas; had this opportunity come earlier, you would not have wandered until today. Now that you are fortunate enough to have this great karmic opportunity, how could you lightly let it pass?]

The confusion of late (referring to the “seeing ghosts in broad daylight” mentioned below), I imagine, has already settled. This matter (the retreat) cannot be done with admixtures; one must lay hold right where the root of life is cut off and simply go on doing it. Do not concern yourself with how he is or how I am: the moment the slightest stray thought remains in the breast, you are toyed with by it. This present opportunity of retreat could not be sought in a hundred thousand kalpas; had this opportunity come earlier, you would not have wandered until today. Now that you are fortunate enough to have this one great karmic opportunity, how could you lightly let it pass?
[The pronoun tuō] It indicates the third person.

[A hundred years of time is but a moment; steal these three years of work, and they pass in the blink of an eye. Set your teeth and clench your jaw, and a turn of the head is all it takes. Do what you can while you can. After three years, let it be as it will: even if you do not awaken to the Way, you will at least have fulfilled the original intent with which you began to study the Way. This is the first step out of birth and death — how can you beat the retreat drum the moment you step out the door? From now on, truly put it down and pay no more heed to how it goes. Even amid swords and spears one must let go of body and life — how much more so when, on level ground in broad daylight, one sees ghosts and gives rise to inverted thoughts? Do not doubt; you must simply cut it off. Rouse your spirit; do not be entangled by it.]

A hundred years of time is but a moment; to draw out three years for retreat passes in the blink of an eye. Whatever difficulties you meet, set your teeth and clench your jaw — a turn of the head (a change of heart) is all it takes. Do what you can while you can, and only leave the retreat when the three years are up; let it be as it will. Even if you do not awaken to the Way, you will have fulfilled the original intent with which you began to study the Way. This is the first step out of birth and death — how can you beat the retreat drum the moment you step out the door? From now on, truly put it down and pay no more heed to how it goes. Even amid swords and spears one must lay down body and life — how much more so when, on level ground in broad daylight, one sees ghosts and gives rise to inverted thoughts? Do not doubt; you must simply cut it off (the doubt). Rouse your spirit; do not be entangled by it.
[To steal (tōu)] To draw out time; for example: to steal a moment of leisure, to snatch spare time, to steal leisure.

[Again: the long rains oppress one, and I have not been able to send word; this mind of mine has never for a single thought let you go. I know that you dwell at ease in quiet and that body and mind are peaceful, so that stray thoughts have long since of themselves melted away. But in the midst of stray thoughts melting away there comes of itself a lightness and ease and happiness — and one must not take that lightness and ease as the thing to be enjoyed. If you take it as attainment, then from that point you fall into the illness of letting things be, seeking only a dim, continuous vacancy and taking having nothing to do as wonderful. You little know that this illness is the most poisonous of all: if you hold to it long, there will be no progress at all; ignorance will secretly grow, karmic consciousness will flow on, the root of life will not be cut off, and in the end it is like wiping quicksilver with spittle — utterly useless.]

Again: the long rains oppress one and news is cut off; this mind of mine has never for a single thought let you go. I know that you dwell at ease in quiet and that body and mind are peaceful, so that stray thoughts have long since melted away. In the midst of stray thoughts melting away there comes of itself a lightness and ease and happiness, but one must by no means take that lightness and ease as the thing to be enjoyed. If you take it as attainment, then from that point you fall into the illness of letting things be, seeking only a dim, continuous vacancy and taking having nothing to do as wonderful. You little know that this illness is the most poisonous of all: if you hold to it long, there will be no progress at all; ignorance will secretly grow, karmic consciousness will flow on, the root of life will not be cut off, and in the end it is like wiping quicksilver with spittle — utterly useless.

[The illness of letting things be] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Second, the illness of letting things be. If there is a person who speaks thus — ‘We now do not cut off birth and death, nor seek nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa and birth and death have no thought of arising or ceasing; let everything be as it will, following the nature of all dharmas’ — and wishes thereby to seek perfect enlightenment: because the nature of perfect enlightenment is not something that comes from letting be, this is called an illness.” On this Master Hanshan comments: “This sets forth the illness of letting things be. This illness of letting be belongs to people of wild understanding, who drift on in heedless self-will, indulging body and mind, claiming that they are without things and without obstruction and have attained great liberation, and who further borrow the words that originally there is no birth and death to cut off and no nirvāṇa to realize, making them provision for self-indulgence. They are not good friends of true knowledge and view. If one follows such people, one falls into wild delusion; hence it is said that self-willed letting be is an illness.” (Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment) [Wiping quicksilver with spittle] This is the so-called “secret formula” of the elixir of immortality, which in fact has no efficacy; hence Master Hanshan uses it here as a metaphor for something utterly useless.

[When stray thoughts melt away, that is precisely the time to put forth effort and take up the huatou, investigating earnestly and laying on the mass of doubt afresh. If the mass of doubt gains power and you hold firmly to the huatou, examining it day and night, investigating more and more deeply, there will at last come the time when cold ashes burst into beans. If you settle on having nothing to do and do not raise the mass of doubt, it is in the end not true practice. The Recorded Sayings of Gaofeng is just the right teacher — and do not take it as a mysterious principle. Strive on! Strive on!]

When stray thoughts melt away, that is precisely the time to put forth effort and take up the huatou, investigating earnestly and laying on the mass of doubt afresh. If the mass of doubt gains power and you hold firmly to the huatou, examining it day and night, investigating more and more deeply, there will at last come the time when cold ashes burst into beans (when the black lacquer barrel is smashed and the original face is seen through). If you settle on having nothing to do and do not raise the mass of doubt, it is in the end not true practice. The Recorded Sayings of Gaofeng is just the right teacher — but do not take it as a mysterious principle. Strive on! Strive on!

[Chan Master Gaofeng] His posthumous name was Yuanmiao. He was born in the wuxu year of the Jiaxi era of the Song dynasty, and attained the Dharma under Yunyan Qin at Beijian. In the jimao year of the Zhiyuan era of Kublai Khan, he went up the West Peak of Mount Tianmu and entered Zhanggong Cave, inscribing it “the Death Barrier”; he did not go out of doors for fifteen years. Students came to consult him without a single day’s gap. His Recorded Sayings of Gaofeng circulates widely in the world.
From Master Hanshan’s Dream-Wandering Collection: To Bao Zhongsu of the Ministry of Rites
[You have written to tell me that in your recent practice you have gradually found an entry into your original ground, and that you would like a single secret phrase to serve as a shortcut.]

You have written that in your recent practice you have gradually found an entry into your original ground, and that you hope I will tell you a single secret phrase to serve as a shortcut to seeing your own nature.

[Original ground (běn dì)] As against the manifested transformation body, the source from which it is manifested is called the original ground. Here it means the original nature, what the Chan school calls one’s original face.

[Fundamentally this matter is originally neither secret nor not secret; it depends only on working at the single thought of the person concerned. Even the one device of watching the huatou is used only because there is no other way. One need only see through, with all one’s strength, the mind of perception that appears before one in daily life — it is all the working of deluded thought. Even if there are mysterious and wondrous views and understandings, they are all shadows of the spirit of consciousness, all matters on the side of mind, consciousness, and ideation. In short, one has never understood the one device of transcending mind, consciousness, and ideation; hence every movement of mind and arising of thought falls into the old trap of deluded thought. Therefore the Buddha said: All sentient beings, because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, employ various deluded thoughts; these thoughts being untrue, they turn round in birth and death. This is also what Aśvaghoṣa said: All sentient beings, from the very beginning, have never been apart from thought.]

Fundamentally, this matter (seeing one’s own nature) is originally neither secret nor not secret; the key is to work at one’s own single present thought. Even the one device of watching the huatou is used only because there is no other way. One need only see through, with all one’s strength, the mind of perception that appears before one in daily life — it is all the working of deluded thought. Even if there are mysterious and wondrous views and understandings, they too are all shadows of the spirit of consciousness, all matters on the side of mind, consciousness, and ideation. In short, one has never understood the one device of transcending mind, consciousness, and ideation; hence every movement of mind and arising of thought falls into the old trap of deluded thought. So in the Śūraṃgama Sutra the Buddha says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure and luminous substance of the nature (all because they do not know this pure and luminous substance of the nature that permanently abides in the true mind), and employ various deluded thoughts (and instead follow deluded thoughts); these thoughts being untrue, they turn round in birth and death.” This is also what Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa says in the Awakening of Faith: all sentient beings, from the very beginning, have never been apart from thought.

[Mind, consciousness, and ideation] “Mind” means collecting and giving rise to, and refers to the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna). “Consciousness” (yì) means thinking and measuring, and refers to the seventh consciousness (manas). “Ideation” (shí) means distinguishing, and refers to the sixth consciousness (mental consciousness). [The old trap (kē jiù)] An old pattern, a worn rut. [The pure and luminous substance of the nature] The luminous, wondrous substance whose nature is originally pure. Grammatically, “pure nature, luminous substance” is in apposition, modifying the noun “true mind.” “Pure nature”: the nature is originally pure, without bondage or defilement. “Luminous substance”: the luminous and wondrous essence. [Turning round] Fragmented birth and death and transformative birth and death. [Fragmented birth and death] For sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because of the karma of good and evil they are moved by, their life spans are all limited and their bodies are all distinct; hence their birth and death is called “fragmented birth and death.” One who ends fragmented birth and death escapes the round of rebirth. [Transformative birth and death] For the sages of the three vehicles, who have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended fragmented birth and death: in the course of practice, deluded thought gradually ceases and realized awakening gradually increases. Each period of this movement between delusion and awakening is different; the passage from the preceding period into the following one is just like a single birth and death, and its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable — hence it is called “transformative birth and death.” One who ends transformative birth and death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Know then that all the various deluded thoughts that sentient beings use in daily life are, in the end, only a single deluded thought! And this single thought is precisely the first source from which delusion arose; from beginningless time until now it has been only this single thought, with no second. Even mind, consciousness, and ideation all arise from this single thought. So if in the practice you now do you can see through this single thought, then all deluded thoughts and emotional calculations will at once be clear as ice. This is what is meant by “one who is apart from the mark of thought is equal to the realm of empty space.”]

From this we know that all the various deluded thoughts that sentient beings use in daily life are, in the end, only a single deluded thought! And this single thought is precisely the first source from which delusion arose; from beginningless time until now it has been only this single thought, with no second. Even mind, consciousness, and ideation always arise from this single thought. So if in the practice you do now you can see through this single thought, then all deluded thoughts and emotional calculations will at once vanish like mist! This is what the Awakening of Faith says: “One who is apart from the mark of thought is equal to the realm of empty space.”

[Yet because sentient beings see only the deluded thoughts in their minds, so numerous and tangled, they in fact do not know that it is only one thought. Now, since deluded thoughts are unavoidably tangled, the ancients taught people to take up a single huatou as their practice. When you go to the bottom of it, even the huatou is a deluded thought; it is simply that one uses this single thought of the huatou to dam up stray thoughts and bring them back to one. If one investigates this single thought thoroughly, gazing deep into it, gazing and gazing, one finds it has originally no place of arising and is of itself unborn. Once one suddenly understands that a single thought is unborn, then the root of emotion from time without beginning is at once released — this is called awakening; it is not that there is some separate mystery to be awakened to.]

Yet because sentient beings see only the deluded thoughts in their minds, so numerous and tangled, they in fact do not know that it is only one thought. Now, since deluded thoughts are unavoidably tangled, the ancients taught people to take up a single huatou as their practice. Ultimately, even the huatou is a deluded thought; it is simply that one uses this single thought of the huatou to dam up stray thoughts and bring them back to one. If one investigates this single thought thoroughly, gazing deep into it, gazing and gazing, one finds it has originally no place of arising and is of itself unborn. Once one suddenly understands that a single thought is unborn, then the root of emotion from time without beginning is at once released — this is called awakening; it is not that there is some separate mystery to be awakened to.

[They in fact do not know that it is only one thought] It is like a single monkey in a forest, leaping from this tree to that, leaping back and forth, so that it seems there are many monkeys each in its own tree, when in fact it is only this one monkey leaping very fast. Hence the method for stilling delusion is to tether this monkey to the tree of right mindfulness, so as to bring the ten thousand thoughts back to one, and then bring the one back to nothing. [Bring them back to one] Watching the mind and watching the huatou are both the work of bringing the ten thousand thoughts back to one.

[I hope that in your practice now, old layman, at the point where you take up the huatou with effort, you will put your effort only into watching this single thought, pursuing it deeply, until you suddenly see that this single thought has originally no place of birth. If you understand that a single thought is unborn, then from that point every thought is unborn — this is what the Sixth Patriarch meant by “dwelling on nothing, yet giving rise to mind.” If you seek the mysterious and wondrous, then you are dwelling on something!]

I hope that in your practice now, old layman, at the point where you take up the huatou with effort, you will put your effort only into watching this single thought, pursuing it deeply, until you suddenly see that this single thought has originally no place of birth. If you understand that a single thought is unborn, then from that point every thought is unborn — this is what the Sixth Patriarch meant by “dwelling on nothing, yet giving rise to mind.” If you seek the mysterious and wondrous, then you are dwelling on something!

[Such a direct and immediate point is the most powerful; it does not lie in seeking much knowledge and view. In this not a single word is of use. One need only first put down all the deluded thoughts and views in one’s breast, until the mind is empty and free and easy, not a thread remaining; then watch where a thought arises and put forth effort to pursue it. This is to go straight in single-handed, allowing no reckoning ahead or behind, no calculations of any kind. The moment there is reckoning, you are far, far away.]

Such a direct and immediate point is the most powerful; it does not lie in seeking much knowledge and view. In this practice not a single word is of use. One need only first put down all the deluded thoughts and views in one’s breast, until the mind is empty and free and easy, not a thread remaining; then watch where a thought arises and put forth effort to pursue it. This is to go straight in single-handed, allowing no reckoning ahead or behind, no calculations of any kind. The moment there is reckoning, you are far, far away from seeing your own nature.
[Old layman, since you have set your will on this matter, how would it be to try setting to work in this way?]
Old layman, since you have set your will on this matter (seeing one’s own nature), how would it be to try setting to work in this way?
The Dream-Wandering Collection: Essential Instructions on Buddha-Recitation and Chan Practice

The public case of investigating the Buddha-recitation is this: one simply takes up the single sound of Amitābha Buddha as the huatou, and at the very point of taking it up lays on the mass of doubt, asking intently
that is
who it is that recites the Buddha. Take it up again and examine it again, examine it over and over, and see who it is, in the end, that recites the Buddha.

The so-called public case of investigating the Buddha-recitation is simply taking up the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” as the huatou, and at the very point of taking it up laying on the mass of doubt, asking intently (gazing into) who it is that recites the Buddha. Take it up again and examine it again, examine it over and over, until you see who it is, in the end, that recites the Buddha.

[The public case of investigating the Buddha-recitation] This is the investigation “Who recites the Buddha?” [At once laying on the mass of doubt, asking intently who it is that recites the Buddha] To ask intently is to gaze deeply into it, not to use the mind of consciousness to think and conjecture.
Master Hanshan says:
‘To investigate the Buddha-recitation as spoken of here means to aim at wondrous awakening
(seeing one’s own nature)
, that is, to take the single sound of the Buddha as a huatou and investigate it — what is called the public case of Buddha-recitation and Chan practice.
One need only raise the single sound of the Buddha, and at once doubt and ask: who is it?
Gaze deeply into it

: from where does this Buddha arise, and who is it, in the end, that recites? Doubting in this way, doubting back and forth, investigating again and again, after a long time gaining power, one suddenly awakens
(sees one’s own nature)
(The Dream-Wandering Collection: Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou)

Holding firmly to the huatou in this way, all deluded thoughts and stray notions are at once cut off, like cutting through tangled silk; they are no longer allowed to arise, and wherever they arise they dissolve. There remains only this single thought, clear and solitary, like the white sun in the empty sky; deluded thoughts do not arise, and confusion of itself retreats — still and yet alert.

Holding firmly to the huatou in this way, all deluded thoughts and stray notions are at once cut off, like cutting through tangled silk. Deluded thoughts and stray notions are no longer allowed to arise again; if they do arise, they are dissolved at the point of arising. There remains only the single thought of the huatou, clear and solitary, like the white sun in the empty sky; deluded thoughts do not arise, and confusion of itself retreats — still and yet alert.
“There remains only this single thought, clear and solitary” — this is the state of the ten thousand thoughts returning to one.
Master Yongjia says:
Still and yet alert, this is right; still and yet blank, this is wrong. Alert and yet still, this is right; alert and yet lost in thought, this is wrong.
That is to say: still without falling into torpor or blankness, alert without falling into deluded thought; stillness and alertness flow together, and both sinking and floating are relinquished.

Master Yongjia said: ‘Still and yet alert is right; still and yet torpid (blank) is wrong. Alert and yet still is right; alert and yet lost in thought is wrong.’ That is to say: still without falling into torpor, alert without falling into deluded thought; stillness and alertness walk together, and both sinking and floating are relinquished.

[Still (jì jì)] Without thought. [Alert (xīng xīng)] The spirit clear and awake. [Blankness (wú jì)] Torpor. [Both sinking and floating relinquished] “Sinking” means blankness; “floating” means deluded thought.
Watch
(gaze into and investigate)
until you reach the place where not a single thought arises: then the preceding and following reaches are cut off, and the middle stands alone of itself.]

Practicing in this way, gazing into it until you reach the place where not a single thought arises, the preceding and following thoughts are cut off and the middle stands alone of itself. (This is the state of the one returning to nothing.)

[The preceding and following reaches are cut off] The preceding thought and the following thought are at once cut off. The Commentary of Jingying says: “Conditioned dharmas arise one after another. The former is the former reach, the latter the latter reach.” The Record of the Mirror of the Source says: “If not a single thought arises, then the preceding and following reaches are cut off. The illuminating substance stands alone; things and self are both thus; one goes straight to the source of mind.” [The illuminating substance stands alone] Apart from delusion and cut off from marks, the illuminating substance (the original nature) stands alone. [Things and self] Outer things and one’s own body. [Thus (rú)] The true, unchanging original nature of all things. This nature is extremely hard to describe in words, and so the word “thus” is borrowed to represent it. The original nature is true reality, and true reality is “thus”: because it is non-dual, unchanging, immutable, and unmoving, and because the true face of all dharmas is one and the same mark (the true reality of all dharmas), it is named “thus.” [Going straight to the source of mind] Going straight to the original nature. “The source of mind” here means the true suchness of the original nature.

The Treatise on the Essence of the Universe and All Things says: “The preceding and following reaches are cut off, and the paths of mind come to an end. One thought for ten thousand years, forever and ever illuminating. Alert and yet still, without delusion and without torpor; bright and clear, with substance and with function. Diligent and unremitting, straight on to the unborn. When the melon is ripe the stem falls — cold and warmth one knows for oneself.” (Translation: the preceding and following thoughts are cut off, and the paths of mind are ended. Maintaining this state of not a single thought arising for a long time, forever and ever illuminating. Alert and yet still, without deluded thought and without torpor; bright and clear, with substance and with function. Diligent and unremitting, straight on to no birth and no death. Suddenly the black lacquer barrel is smashed, and one at once sees one’s original face, like a person drinking water, knowing for oneself whether it is cold or warm.)

[Suddenly the black lacquer barrel is smashed, and one at once sees one’s original face. Then body, mind, and world at once sink away, like the shadows of sky-flowers falling; the ten directions are perfectly clear, becoming one great treasury of light. Only then is it the season of arriving home: in daily life before one, all is bright and perfectly clear, with nothing further to doubt. Only then does one believe that one’s own mind was originally thus. It is no different in the slightest from the ground of self-enjoyment of the Buddhas and patriarchs of former times.

Suddenly the black lacquer barrel is smashed, and one at once sees one’s original face (sees through to the original nature). Then body, mind, and world at once sink out of sight, the illusory shadows of sky-flowers cease, the ten directions are perfectly clear, becoming one great treasury of light. Only then is it the season of arriving home: in daily life before one, all is bright and perfectly clear, with nothing further to doubt. Only then does one believe that one’s own mind was originally thus. This is entirely the same (no different in the slightest) as the ground of self-enjoyment of the Buddhas of former times.

[Sink away] Also written “sink and submerge”: to sink, to disappear. [Treasury of light] A treasury of light; it refers to the body of the Tathāgata. The Sutra of Viśeṣacintī says: “The body of the Tathāgata is the treasury of immeasurable light.”
“Suddenly the black lacquer barrel is smashed, and one at once sees one’s original face” — this is the state of understanding the mind and seeing the nature.

Having reached this state, one must not take it as a view of emptiness. If one takes it as a view of emptiness, one falls into the evil views of outside teachings. Nor may one make it a view of existence, nor a mysterious and wondrous view and understanding. Any view at all at once falls into wrong view. If in the course of practice various states appear, by no means acknowledge them; one shout and they dissolve. Evil states need not be feared, good states need not be delighted in — these are the demons of habitual tendency. If you give rise to worry or joy, you fall among demons. You should contemplate that they are only manifestations of your own mind and do not come from outside. You should know that it is originally pure, that in the mind there is not a single thing, that there is originally neither delusion nor awakening, and that it does not belong to sage or ordinary being — how then could there be any states at all?

Having reached this state, one must not take it as a view of emptiness. If one takes it as a view of emptiness, one falls into the evil views of outside teachings. Nor may one make it a view of existence, nor a mysterious and wondrous view and understanding. So long as there is any view at all, one falls into wrong view. If in the course of practice various states appear, by no means take them as real; one shout (a scolding) and they dissolve. Evil states need not be feared, good states need not be delighted in — these are the demons of habitual tendency. If you give rise to worry or joy, you fall among demons. You should contemplate that all states are only manifestations of your own mind and do not come from outside. You should know that your own mind is originally pure, with not a single thing in it, that there is originally neither delusion nor awakening, and that it does not belong to sage or ordinary being — how then could there be any states at all?

It is only because we are deluded about this original mind that we must do the work, so as to wear away the habitual tendencies of ignorance. If one awakens to the original mind as originally without things, originally luminous, vast, pure, and serene, and so lets things take their course as time passes, what work is there left to do?]
It is
only
because
we are deluded about this original mind
that
we must do the work,
so as to
wear away the habitual tendencies of ignorance
, nothing more
. If we awaken to
the
original mind as being without things, originally luminous, vast, pure, and serene, and thus let things take their course
day by day
, what work is there left to do
at all

[If people today would only believe that this mind is originally without things: the reason we do the work now is solely that we have not yet seen our original face, and so we cannot but put in a spell of dead-hard work before there is a season of arriving home. Go straight on from there, and in time you will naturally, suddenly see your original face — this is leaving birth and death
and never again doubting.
If people today would only believe that this mind is originally without things, then as for the practice we now do, we
only
do it
because
we have not yet seen our original face, and so we cannot but put in a spell of dead-hard work before there is a season of arriving home. Go straight on from
this point
forward, and naturally
you will
suddenly see your original face and be done with birth and death
never again doubting.

How is it that investigation is precisely Buddha-recitation, and Buddha-recitation is precisely investigation? The investigation spoken of now is simply taking the single phrase “Amitābha” as the huatou and making it the work of close inquiry. Put down all at once your own body, mind, and world, together with all your former worldly truths
conventional and habitual speech

and Buddhadharma views and understandings. Then, from within empty stillness, raise up with effort the single sound of Amitābha Buddha, clear and distinct. Just as you raise it, look directly into it and inquire closely: who is it that recites the Buddha? Lay on the mass of doubt again, examine it over and over, doubt it again and again, like a donkey gazing into a well.
How can it be that investigation is
precisely
Buddha-recitation, and Buddha-recitation is
precisely
investigation
at all
It
is
simply to
take the single phrase ‘Amitābha
Buddha
and make it
the huatou,
and so
do the work of close inquiry. Put down all at once
your
body and mind
and

conventional and habitual speech

and Buddhadharma views and understandings. Then, from within empty stillness, raise up with effort the single sound of Amitābha Buddha, clear and distinct. Just as you raise it, look directly into it and inquire closely: who is it that recites the Buddha? Lay on the mass of doubt again (the ‘mass of doubt’ spoken of here means concentrating the spirit to look into and investigate: who is it that recites the Buddha?), examine it over and over (the ‘examination’ spoken of here means looking into and investigating), doubt it again and again, like a donkey gazing into a well.
[Worldly truth] Also called conventional truth; it means the truth of the world, and also refers to the principles known to worldly people. [Like a donkey gazing into a well] It is like a donkey
staring stupidly at the water in a well,
a metaphor for looking and gazing
in a way
that transcends emotional consciousness and discrimination. The Record of Caoshan says:
‘The Master
(Chan Master Caoshan Benji Yuanzheng)
asked the senior monk De: “The Buddha’s true dharma-body is like empty space; it responds to things by manifesting forms, like the moon in water. How would you speak of the principle of this response
(how should one speak of this principle)
?” De said: “Like a donkey gazing into a well.” The Master said: “You have spoken only eighty percent of it.” De said: “How would you speak of it, Reverend
(Reverend, how would you put it)
?” The Master said: “Like a well gazing at the donkey.”’
